title: Sections at an algebraically closed point commute with finite coefficient reduction
statement:
Let $\kappa$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-algebraic-closure], $t=\operatorname{Spec}\kappa$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] with its small pro-etale site $t_{\mathrm{proet}}$ [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site], and let $\Gamma(t,-)$ be the sections over the final object $\operatorname{id}_t$, on derived categories [lem-weil-point-proetale-sections-exact]. Fix a prime $\ell$ invertible in $\kappa$, a finite extension $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ with valuation ring $\mathcal O_E$ and uniformizer $\varpi_E$, and put $A_i=\mathcal O_E/\varpi_E^i$ for $i\geq1$ [def-weil-l-adic-coefficient-extension]. Write $(A_i)_t$ for the constant sheaf of rings on $t_{\mathrm{proet}}$ [def-weil-pbc-constant-sheaf], so that $\Gamma(t,(A_i)_t)=A_i$, and $D(t_{\mathrm{proet}},A_i)$, $D(A_i)$ for the derived categories of $(A_i)_t$-modules and of $A_i$-modules [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Let $n\geq j\geq1$ and let $N\in D(t_{\mathrm{proet}},A_n)$ have cohomology sheaves vanishing in all sufficiently large degrees (in particular, $N$ may be cohomologically bounded). This bounded-above domain is preserved by the reductions below. Let $N\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{A_n}A_j\in D(t_{\mathrm{proet}},A_j)$ be the derived change of rings along $(A_n)_t\to(A_j)_t$, and $\Gamma(t,N)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{A_n}A_j\in D(A_j)$ the derived change of rings along $A_n\to A_j$, both as in [lem-pur-derived-change-of-rings]. Then there is an isomorphism
$$
\Gamma(t,N)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{A_n}A_j\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Gamma\bigl(t,N\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{A_n}A_j\bigr)
$$
in $D(A_j)$, natural in $N$, equal to the identity for $j=n$, and compatible with successive reductions: for $n\geq j\geq i\geq1$ the isomorphism for $(n,i)$ is the composite of the isomorphism for $(n,j)$ reduced to $A_i$ and the isomorphism for $(j,i)$ applied to $N\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{A_n}A_j$, under the associativity identifications $(-\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{A_n}A_j)\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{A_j}A_i\cong-\otimes^{\mathbf L}_{A_n}A_i$.

proof.text: Put $V=\mathcal O_E$, $\pi=\varpi_E$ and $R=A_n=V/(\pi^n)$. The coefficient-ring theorem says that $V$ is a discrete valuation ring, a principal ideal domain, and every nonzero element is a unit times a power of $\pi$. An ideal $I$ of $R$ pulls back to an ideal $(a)$ of $V$ containing $(\pi^n)$; thus $a$ is a unit times $\pi^r$ for some $0\le r\le n$. Therefore $I=(\pi^r)$ and $R$ is Noetherian. Multiplication by $\pi^r$ identifies $R/(\pi^{n-r})$ with $I$: indeed $\pi^rx\in(\pi^n)$ in $V$ if and only if $x\in(\pi^{n-r})$. This includes $r=0$ (the whole ideal) and $r=n$ (the zero ideal). The same conclusions hold with any positive index in place of $n$.

source.place: Coefficient datum; elementary ideal and annihilator calculation from the DVR theorem. No finite projective dimension over A_n is asserted.

proof.text:
First justify the coefficient identification used in the statement. Give an abelian group $T$ the discrete topology. The continuous-function sheaf theorem makes $L_T(U)=C(|U|,T)$ an fpqc sheaf, hence a sheaf on $t_{\mathrm{proet}}$, since its covers are fpqc. The map from the constant presheaf to $L_T$ exhibits it as the constant sheaf: a continuous function $f:|U|\to T$ has open fibres $U_a=f^{-1}(a)$ forming a Zariski, hence pro-etale, cover; a map from the constant presheaf to any sheaf extends uniquely by gluing its constant sections on these fibres. Pullback of the fibres proves compatibility with restriction, and uniqueness follows on this cover. This is exactly the universal property of sheafification. For a ring $T$, pointwise operations give the same identification as ring sheaves. Since $|t|$ is a singleton, evaluation gives $\Gamma(t,T_t)=T$, preserving constant sections and all coefficient maps. Apply this to every $A_m$ and to the zero quotient when it occurs below.

For any sheaf $F$ of $R_t$-modules and $0\le r\le n$, the constant-module exactness theorem, applicable because $R$ is Noetherian, turns $R\xrightarrow{\pi^r}R\to R/(\pi^r)\to0$ into the corresponding exact sequence of constant sheaves. By the balanced tensor universal property, $F\otimes_{R_t}(R/(\pi^r))_t=F/\pi^rF$: the maps are $x\otimes\bar a\mapsto ax\bmod\pi^rF$ and $\bar x\mapsto x\otimes1$, locally on sections and hence after sheafification. Write $J=\pi^rF=\operatorname{im}(\pi^r:F\to F)$. Exact sections of $F\twoheadrightarrow J$ show $\Gamma(t,J)=\pi^r\Gamma(t,F)$ inside $\Gamma(t,F)$; exact sections of $0\to J\to F\to F/J\to0$ then give a natural $R/(\pi^r)$-linear isomorphism
$$\eta_{r,F}:\Gamma(t,F)/\pi^r\Gamma(t,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(t,F/\pi^rF).$$
It sends the class of a global section to its quotient section. This argument also proves the identification with $\Gamma(t,F)\otimes_R R/(\pi^r)$, by the same two mutually inverse balanced maps for ordinary modules.

proof.text:
If $F$ is flat over $R_t$, then $\Gamma(t,F)$ is flat over $R$. To verify this, let $I=(\pi^r)$ be any ideal as in step 1. Constant exactness gives an injection $I_t\to R_t$ and identifies $I_t$ with $(R/(\pi^{n-r}))_t$. Tensoring this injection with $F$ is injective by the definition of flatness; its source is $F/\pi^{n-r}F$ and its map to $F$ is multiplication by $\pi^r$. Apply exact sections and step 2 to obtain an injection
$$\Gamma(t,F)/\pi^{n-r}\Gamma(t,F)\longrightarrow\Gamma(t,F),\qquad\bar x\longmapsto\pi^rx.$$
Under $I=R/(\pi^{n-r})$ this is exactly $I\otimes_R\Gamma(t,F)\to\Gamma(t,F)$. The finitely generated ideal criterion for flatness now proves the claim. No assertion that an arbitrary module sheaf is constant is used.

proof.text: Choose a complex $M$ representing $N$ and an integer $b$ above its nonzero cohomology. Replace $M$ by the complex equal to $M^q$ for $q<b$, to $\ker(d_M^b)$ in degree $b$, and to zero above $b$. Its inclusion in $M$ is a quasi-isomorphism: cohomology is unchanged below $b$, is $H^b(M)$ in degree $b$, and is zero above $b$ on both sides. The bounded-above flat replacement theorem supplies $P\to M$ with $P^q=0$ for $q>b$, flat terms and a quasi-isomorphism (here $M$ denotes this truncated representative). The site K-flatness criterion makes $P$ K-flat. Put $C=\Gamma(t,P)$. Exact point sections show that $C$ represents $\Gamma(t,N)$, and step 3 makes every $C^q$ flat over $R$. Since $C$ is bounded above, the ordinary-module K-flatness criterion makes $C$ K-flat too.

proof.text:
Let $B=A_j=R/(\pi^j)$. Derived change of rings on the site, computed using $P$, represents $N\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}B$ by the actual complex of $B_t$-modules $P_j=P\otimes_{R_t}B_t=P/\pi^jP$. Ordinary derived tensor, computed using the K-flat complex $C$, represents $\Gamma(t,N)\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}B$ by $C\otimes_R B=C/\pi^jC$ as a complex of $B$-modules. Applying step 2 in every degree gives a chain isomorphism
$$\eta_{j,P}:C/\pi^j C\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(t,P/\pi^jP).$$
It commutes with differentials because it sends $[x]$ to the quotient of $x$. This produces the required isomorphism in $D(B)$ itself, with its $B$-action, rather than only an isomorphism after forgetting to $D(R)$.

proof.text: Here are choice independence and naturality on the bounded-above derived category. On bounded-above complexes use the functorial flat replacement $M\mapsto P(M)$ supplied by the replacement theorem. For a chain map $f:M\to M'$, the degreewise quotient-to-sections maps give a commuting square for $P(f)$. If $f$ is a quasi-isomorphism, so is $P(f)$ by its natural augmentation; the two sides of the square become isomorphisms, by derived change of rings and exact sections. Thus these squares descend through localization and remain commuting when a quasi-isomorphism is inverted. To justify using bounded-above representatives for every derived morphism, apply the bounded-below cochain localization theorem to the opposite abelian category and reverse degrees: $K^r\mapsto(K^{-r})^{\mathrm{op}}$, with reversed differentials. This exchanges bounded below with bounded above, preserves the quasi-isomorphism condition (kernels and cokernels are exchanged), and identifies the opposite derived localization with the localization of the reversed complexes by its universal property. It gives precisely localization of bounded-above complexes onto $D^-$. The localization universal property therefore yields a natural isomorphism on $D^-$. Finally for any other bounded-above flat resolution $S\to M$, the natural maps $P(S)\to S$ and $P(S)\to P(M)$ are quasi-isomorphisms between bounded-above flat complexes. The commuting quotient-to-sections squares for these two maps identify the comparison computed with $S$ with the descended comparison. Hence the comparison is independent of the resolution and natural in every derived morphism of $N$.

proof.text: The reduced model $P_j$ is again bounded above and has flat $B_t$-module terms. Indeed for an injection $U\to V$ of $B_t$-modules the maps $U\otimes_{B_t}(P^q\otimes_{R_t}B_t)\to V\otimes_{B_t}(P^q\otimes_{R_t}B_t)$ identify with $U\otimes_{R_t}P^q\to V\otimes_{R_t}P^q$ by $u\otimes(x\otimes b)\mapsto bu\otimes x$ and its inverse $u\otimes x\mapsto u\otimes(x\otimes1)$. They are injective by flatness of $P^q$; the same formulas and exactness prove tensor-flatness over $B_t$. The site K-flatness criterion applies to $P_j$. Step 3 with $j$ in place of $n$ makes $\Gamma(t,P_j)$ termwise flat over $B$, and the ordinary K-flatness criterion applies to this bounded-above complex. In particular both reduced objects are bounded above; this explains the domain chosen in the statement and makes the next successive reduction legitimate.

source.place: Tag 06YQ, lemma-bounded-flat-K-flat; more-algebra.tex Tag 064K. Flatness under scalar extension is the displayed balanced-map calculation from the definition of flatness.

proof.text: For $j=n$, $\pi^n$ acts as zero and the quotient-to-sections map is the identity of $C$, under the usual unit identifications. For $n\ge j\ge i\ge1$, use the single model $P$ and its reduced model $P_j$ of step 7. Both successive derived tensor operations are computed by ordinary quotients on these models, including on the ordinary-module side. The associators are the maps $((x\otimes b)\otimes c)\mapsto x\otimes bc$; equivalently $(P/\pi^jP)/\pi^i(P/\pi^jP)=P/\pi^iP$, and likewise for $C$. The direct quotient-to-sections map sends the class of $x\in\Gamma(t,P^q)$ to its class in $\Gamma(t,P^q/\pi^iP^q)$. The comparison for $(n,j)$ reduced to $A_i$, followed by the comparison for $(j,i)$ on $P_j$, sends $[[x]]$ to exactly that same class. The maps are therefore equal degreewise as $A_i$-linear maps, commute with the differentials, and are equal in $D(A_i)$. Choice independence from step 6 identifies these model computations with the asserted natural isomorphisms. This proves identity and successive-reduction compatibility without assigning an $A_j$-action to a free resolution over $A_n$.

Statement: the original text was created by Q78 for bounded objects. The change to bounded-above objects is correct and makes the statement stronger, not weaker. Over A_2, Tor_r(A_1,A_1)=A_1 for every r, so the old successive-reduction clause applied its own comparison to an unbounded object. The only citer uses the item in its steps 1 and 7 on bounded Ra_{X!}K_{n+1} and L ybar^*K_{n+1}, so nothing breaks. Steps: (1) the ideals of V/pi^n are the (pi^r), and multiplication by pi^r gives R/pi^{n-r} isomorphic to (pi^r). (2) A discrete constant sheaf is sheafified as continuous functions, using the fpqc-sheaf leaf, open fibres as a Zariski cover and the universal property, so Gamma(t,T_t)=T; then F tensor (R/pi^r)_t = F/pi^rF, and exact sections give eta. (4) Good truncation and the bounded-above flat replacement make P and C=Gamma(P) K-flat. (5) The chain isomorphism C/pi^jC -> Gamma(P/pi^jP) is B-linear. (6) Naturality comes from the bounded-below localization node applied in the opposite category, then the localization universal property (2); resolution independence via P(S). (7) P_j stays termwise flat over B_t and bounded above. (8) Both routes send [[x]] to the class of x; j=n gives the identity. Edge cases checked: zero object and shifts, n=j=i=1, j=n, i=j, r=0 and r=n, and empty site objects. The hypothesis 'l invertible in kappa' is unused but harmless.
